---
order: 5
unit: core
title: Who is it for?
summary: "Two things shape how formal to be: how well you know the person (familiarity) and who has more authority (power). Knowing someone well can make words more relaxed; their authority can keep them respectful. Both matter, along with the purpose."
language: maths
node: [AC9E6LA01 n2]
explainPicture: { ref: text.yml#explain-pic, caption: "Three people, three sets of words. How well you know them and how much authority they have both change what you say." }
hook: "Two messages ask for the same favour, one to a cousin and one to a stranger who runs the hall. Would the words match?"
---
Two things shape how formal your words should be.

- **Familiarity**: how well you know the person. Close friends get relaxed words.
- **Power**: who has more authority in the situation. A principal, a judge or a coach can decide things about you.

The two cues can agree or pull in different directions. Think about both before you choose words.

## Predict: friend or boss?

```step
stage: predict
insight: "Predicting how to start a message to a well-known coach previews that familiarity and power both matter."
check:
  type: predict
  q: "You email a coach you know really well to ask to miss training. How would you start?"
  options: ["The same as a message to a close friend", "More formally than a friend, but still warmly", "As formally as a letter to a stranger"]
  actual: "More formally than a friend, but still warmly. Because you know the coach well the words can be warm, but because the coach has authority they should also be respectful."
```

## Try: place each situation

```step
stage: run
insight: "Placing six situations on a casual-to-formal scale shows how familiarity and power change the words."
try: { playground: board, starter: "text.yml#run", height: 460 }
hint: ["Who is more important in this situation, you or them?", "How well do you know them?"]
smaller:
  check: { type: question, q: "Which person would you use the most formal words with?", options: ["Your best friend", "A council officer you have never met", "A neighbour your age"], answer: 1, feedback: ["You know your best friend well and they have no authority over you.", null, "A neighbour your age is your equal."], explain: "A council officer you have never met is both unknown and in authority, so the words are the most formal." }
check: { type: board, text: "Place each situation: casual, respectful or formal.", when: "n_right = 6 and n_wrong = 0", explain: "A cousin is casual, a new classmate is casual to respectful, a coach is casual to respectful, a teacher is respectful to formal, and the mayor and a judge are formal." }
```

## Worked example: familiarity or power?

```step
stage: investigate
insight: "Sorting cues into familiarity and power, spotting reasoning that ignores power and choosing an email opening shows both shape the words."
tasks:
  - check:
      type: sort
      q: "Is each cue about familiarity (how well you know them) or power (their authority)?"
      options: ["Familiarity", "Power"]
      items:
        - ["They are your best friend.", "Familiarity", "It is about how well you know them."]
        - ["They are the principal.", "Power", "It is about their authority."]
        - ["You have never met them.", "Familiarity", "It is about how well you know them."]
        - ["They mark your work.", "Power", "It is about their authority."]
        - ["You have known them for years.", "Familiarity", "It is about how well you know them."]
        - ["They decide who joins the team.", "Power", "It is about their authority."]
  - check:
      type: bug
      code: "working.txt#nib"
      text: "Here is Nib's reasoning before writing to Ms Rossi, one step at a time. In one step Nib decides how to word the request using only one cue. Click it."
      answer: 3
      fault: logic
      misconception: familiarity-only
      explain: "Step 3 decides using only how well Nib knows Ms Rossi (familiarity). She also has power over Nib's extension, so the words need to be respectful too."
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "Ava has played for her coach for three years and they joke often. She emails him to ask to miss training. Which opening fits?"
      options: ["Hey Coach, I'm skipping Thursday.", "Hi Coach, I hope you're well. Could I please miss training on Thursday?", "Dear Mr Wilson, I respectfully request permission to be absent from Thursday's training session."]
      answer: 1
      feedback: ["It sounds like Ava is telling the coach, not asking.", null, "It is stiff for someone Ava knows well."]
      explain: "Warm because Ava knows the coach well, and a request because the coach has the authority to say yes or no."
```

### Familiarity or power?

```worked
\text{Ask: how well do I know them?} :: Close means more relaxed words.
\text{Ask: who decides?} :: The one with authority gets respect.
\text{Combine them} :: A warm request can be both relaxed and respectful.
```

### Choose the opening

## Vary: choose the greeting

```step
stage: modify
insight: "Choosing the greeting for a friend and for a principal you have not met shows the cues at work."
try: { playground: board, starter: "text.yml#vary", height: 340 }
hint: ["Who is the reader, and how well do you know them?", "Do they have authority?"]
check: { type: board, text: "Choose the greeting that fits each reader.", when: "n_right = 2 and n_wrong = 0", explain: "Dear Ms Chen suits a principal you have never met. Hey! suits a cousin." }
```

## Practise: who would you say it to?

```step
stage: practise
insight: "Placing six readers on the scale applies the two cues to new situations."
try: { playground: board, starter: "text.yml#practise", height: 460 }
hint: ["Who has authority over you?", "Who do you know well?"]
check: { type: board, text: "Place each reader: casual, respectful or formal.", when: "n_right = 6 and n_wrong = 0", explain: "A younger sibling is casual, a neighbour you know a little is casual to respectful, a coach you like is respectful, a librarian you have never met is respectful to formal, and a minister and a school council committee are formal." }
```

## Make: three openings

In your own document, write three openings for three readers: a friend, a coach you know well and the principal. Write two sentences for each, at least six sentences in all. Think about how well you know each person and whether they have authority.

Here is one example, for a friend: "Hey Sam, are you free after school? I found a good spot for the project." Your coach and the principal need different words.

Then swap with a partner. For each opening, say how well the writer knows the person and whether the person has authority.

```step
stage: make
insight: "Writing three openings for three readers puts both cues to use in real messages."
hint: ["Who is each reader, and how well do you know them?", "Who has authority?"]
check: { type: reflect, text: "I wrote three openings for a friend, a coach and the principal, and a partner and I said how well I know each person and whether they have authority." }
```

## In your own writing

```step
stage: make
tier: typical
insight: "Checking a real message against familiarity and power puts the idea to use outside the board."
check: { type: reflect, text: "I looked at a message I wrote and asked how well I know the reader and whether they have authority." }
```

## Wider: addressing people in different places

```step
stage: make
tier: wider
insight: "Comparing how people are addressed in a court and a parliament applies the cues to other settings at the same level."
check:
  type: reasoning
  q: "In a court, a parliament or a big company, people often use titles instead of first names. Give one reason this happens, and say what it shows about power."
  placeholder: "Titles are used because ... This shows ..."
  models:
    - title: "A strong answer"
      text: "Titles show respect for the role, not just the person. They show that the speaker has authority in that place, whoever holds the job."
    - title: "A different view that also works"
      text: "Titles keep the setting fair and formal, so everyone is treated the same way. They show that power comes with the role."
  criteria: ["I gave one reason.", "I said what it shows about power.", "I wrote about the role, not one person."]
  explain: "Titles signal the role and make the authority clear."
```

```teacher
summary: Students learn that familiarity (how well you know someone) and power
  (their authority) both shape how formal to be. They place situations on a
  scale, sort cues, find reasoning that ignores power, choose an email opening,
  choose greetings and write three openings.
time: 45
timing: Predict and Try 8 min · Worked example 12 min · Vary and Practise 10 min
  · Make and own writing 15 min
goals:
  - I can say how well I know someone and whether they have authority.
  - I can choose words that fit both.
  - I can explain why a coach I know well still gets respectful words.
  - I can write openings for three different readers.
struggle: Students use only how well they know the person. Ask 'who decides?' to
  bring in power.
before: >
  Do the Try board yourself: six situations, three bands.


  The one idea: familiarity and power are two separate cues. This lesson covers
  AC9E6LA01 node 2: social distance and power as drivers of register. The term
  **register** is for you; the lesson says 'how formal the words are'.


  Kit's criterion: students explain a choice using both cues. The sort and the
  bug task isolate them; the question combines them.


  The Try board accepts two bands for 'Asking a new classmate to share a table'
  and the Practise board for 'A librarian you have never met', because careful
  students can argue either.


  The Make step is written in the students' own documents; nothing on the site
  reads it. A partner or you should judge whether each opening fits its reader.


  The situations are made up for the lesson.
running:
  - "Try: for each, ask 'how well do you know them, and who decides?'."
  - "Worked example: label each cue before reading the answers."
  - "Make: partners say which cue each opening responds to."
stuck:
  - see: A student writes 'Hey Coach' because they know the coach well.
    ask: Who decides whether you can miss training?
    fix: Warm words suit knowing them well. Respectful words suit their authority.
      Use both.
  - see: A student writes very stiff words to a friend, thinking it is safer.
    ask: Who is reading, and how will they feel?
    fix: Stiff words to a close friend can sound cold. Match the reader.
stretch: "Write one request three times: to a friend, a coach and the principal.
  Underline what changes."
support: Two cards, 'How well I know them' and 'Who decides', placed beside each
  situation.
leads: |
  Next in this course: how words show who you are.
exit:
  q: Name the two cues that shape how formal to be.
  a: How well you know the person (familiarity), and who has more authority
    (power).
explain: >
  Two things shape how formal to be: how well you know the person, and who has
  authority.


  They can pull in different directions, so a message can be warm and
  respectful.
class:
  inquiry:
    q: Why do we word things differently for different people?
    prompts:
      - Ask a friend, a coach and a principal for the same thing.
      - What changes, and why?
    notes: Familiarity and power are two separate cues.
  activities:
    - at: predict
      kind: activity
      title: One request, three readers
      minutes: 5
      do: >
        Pairs act out asking for a day off to a friend, a coach and a principal.
        The class names what changed each time.
      notes: Listen for greetings, please and could.
    - at: investigate
      kind: discussion
      title: Warm and respectful
      minutes: 5
      do: >
        Ask: can words be warm and respectful at once? Collect examples from the
        class.
      notes: Aim for 'yes, because there are two cues'.
  questions:
    - at: investigate
      title: Which cue?
      type: question
      q: A student calls the principal 'Ms Chen' even though they chat often. Which
        cue explains it?
      options:
        - Familiarity
        - Power
        - Neither
      answer: 1
      explain: The principal has authority, so the student is respectful even though
        they know each other.
```

# Nib's reasoning before writing to Ms Rossi, one step at a time.

# region: nib
I need an extension on my history essay.
I know Ms Rossi really well, and we chat about footy every lunchtime.
So I will word my request exactly as I would for a friend.
I will write my message now.
# endregion
